problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3y=4{e}^{3x}.
$$
worked_solution:
First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -3 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)(\lambda -3) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =-1$ or $\lambda =3$, and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-x}+B{e}^{3x}.
$$

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $4{e}^{3x}.$ In this case, the constant factor in the exponent is $3$, which coincides with one of the roots of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha x{e}^{3x},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant that is to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=\alpha (1+3x){e}^{3x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=\alpha (9x+6){e}^{3x}.
$$

We substitute ${y}_{p},$ ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and ${y}_{p}^{″}$ into the ODE and solve for $\alpha :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\alpha (9x+6){e}^{3x}-2(\alpha (1+3x){e}^{3x})-3(\alpha x{e}^{3x}) & =4{e}^{3x} \\ (9x+6-2-6x-3x)\alpha {e}^{3x} & =4{e}^{3x} \\ 4\alpha {e}^{3x} & =4{e}^{3x} \\ 4\alpha  & =4 \\ \alpha  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=x{e}^{3x}.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{-x}+B{e}^{3x}+x{e}^{3x}.
$$
